title: Explaining the faith to others
for: I want to explain what I believe
subtitle: Ten short sessions on explaining the Christian faith with gentleness and respect: listening first, your own story, the gospel, the cross, the resurrection, the Trinity, the Bible, and a statement of your own.
intro: This is the closing track of the LiveWell Academy, in the program called Explain It. It's for anyone who has come to understand what Christians believe and why, and now wants to be able to say it to a friend, a child, a coworker or a skeptic across a table. It has ten sessions of about ten minutes each, and you can take them a day apart or a week apart.

Nothing here teaches a script or a technique for winning people over. The aim is the one Peter gave a scattered church: to be ready with a reason for your hope, and to give it with gentleness and respect. Each session opens one page of the site, then asks one question, gives one thing to do and one verse to keep. The last session asks you to write, in your own words, what you believe and why.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Explaining the faith to others, or meeting with one friend to go through it together. The group is for Christians who understand what they believe and want to be able to say it to others with gentleness and respect. It is the closing track of the Academy, so most people will have come through other tracks first, but nobody needs to have.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It gives people room to practise saying things aloud to one another, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Three to eight people is a good size, and two work just as well. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for ten meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Some meetings invite people to try an explanation aloud. Make that an invitation, never a test: anyone may listen instead, and nobody is graded. The point is to grow easier and more honest in speaking, not to produce performers.

sections.title: The room
body: A kitchen table or a living room works well. Have a Bible for each person and the session open on a phone or printed. Say plainly at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about friends and family who don't believe stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud. Speak about people outside the faith as you would if they were sitting at the table with you.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Five minutes: one person reads the session's verse aloud.
Thirty minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order, leaving room for the questions people bring.
Fifteen minutes: anyone who wants to tries the session's explanation aloud in their own words, and the group says what helped.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words. Nobody has to pray aloud.
Five minutes: name the next session and its one thing to do, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Practising explanations will raise questions the group can't settle in an evening: those who never heard, whether other religions hold any truth, how the cross works. Welcome them. Say what the church has always confessed, and where faithful Christians differ, say that they differ and take no side. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week, or ask a pastor.

Watch for a quieter danger: a group that grows confident by mocking the people who disagree with it. Stop it gently when it starts. The track asks for gentleness and respect, and a group that practises contempt among friends will carry it into every conversation it has outside.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Talking about faith with others brings real pain near the surface: a parent who scorned someone's faith, a marriage where only one believes, a child who has walked away, a friendship lost over an argument. When that comes into the room, stop and listen. Don't hurry to advice, and don't suggest that the right words would have changed everything. Ask whether the person wants the group to go on or to pause, and talk with them afterwards.

If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the authorities, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep for weeks, guilt or fear that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Why Christians speak at all
teaching: Christians have talked about Jesus from the first week, and not because they had something to sell. They believed something had happened that concerned everyone: a crucified man had been raised, and the God of Israel had begun to put the world right. News of that kind is spoken, or it isn't news. Peter, writing to small congregations scattered across what is now Turkey, asked them to be ready for one particular moment: “Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15). The word for defense is apologia, the reasoned account a person gave in court. It answers someone who asked.

The church hasn't always spoken that way, and an honest explainer begins by admitting it. In the eighth century Charlemagne's armies baptized conquered Saxons under threat of execution. Nearer our own day the faith has been pressed on people through manipulation, manufactured urgency, and friendships that turned out to be campaigns. Each of these treats a person as a target instead of a neighbor. Jesus himself let a rich man walk away from him sad, and did not chase him with a better offer. This track asks for something slower: to know what you believe and why, and to say it in a way that leaves the other person free.

open.label: Evangelism: A Bible Study on Sharing Your Faith
open.why: A five-session study on telling the truth about Jesus the way a witness tells it, not the way a salesman closes a deal.

also.label: How Do You Share Your Faith Without Being Pushy?
also.why: A longer guide to speaking about Christ in ordinary friendships without pressure, for the Christian who has been either silent or pushy.

also.label: 1 Peter 3, passage by passage
also.why: The chapter around the verse, explained in plain words, so you can see the slandered church Peter was writing to and what he asked of it.

sessions.question: What has made you hesitant to talk about your faith, and how much of that comes from having seen it done badly?
sessions.do: Write down one way you have seen the faith shared that put you off, and one way that drew you in. Keep the page beside you through the track.

verse.text: But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you.

group.open: When did someone first talk with you about Jesus, and how did it land?
discuss: Peter assumes someone will ask before the Christian answers. What would make a friend want to ask you about your hope?
Why do you think forcing or manipulating belief has so often seemed justified to the people who did it?
What is the difference between being ready to explain and being eager to win?
group.pray: Ask God for readiness and gentleness, and pray by name for one or two people in your life who do not yet believe.

sessions.title: Listening before speaking
teaching: Most explanations fail before they start, because they answer a question nobody asked. James put the order plainly: “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Watch Jesus at a well in Samaria at midday. He begins by asking a woman for a drink, which a Jewish man was not expected to do, and the conversation that follows moves at her pace, through her questions about worship and the mountain her people prayed on. He knows her life, and he doesn't use it as a weapon.

Listening isn't a technique for earning the right to give your speech. It's how you find out who is in front of you. A man who asks why God allows suffering has often buried someone, and a woman who asks about hell may be thinking of her brother. Ask what makes them ask. Ask what they were taught, and what they rejected. Restate their view until they say you've got it right. Many people have never heard a Christian describe their objection fairly, and being understood can matter more to them than any answer.

open.label: John 4, the guided seven-step study
open.why: Walk slowly through the conversation at the well and notice who asks the questions, how Jesus answers each one, and how long he lets the woman lead.

also.label: How to Share Your Faith Without Being Weird
also.why: Practical help for starting with the conversation you're already in, and for saying less than you think you need to.

also.label: I don't believe, but I'm curious
also.why: The page this site gives to the curious unbeliever. Read it as your friend would, to hear the tone they are met with here.

sessions.question: Think of one friend who doesn't believe. What do you actually know about why, in their own words?
sessions.do: Have one conversation this week in which you ask a friend what they think about God or faith, and say nothing about your own view unless they ask.

verse.text: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger

group.open: Who is the best listener you know, and what do they do that others don't?
discuss: Why do you think Jesus began with a request instead of an announcement at the well?
What objection to the faith have you heard most often, and could you state it in a form the person would agree with?
What is the difference between listening to someone and waiting for your turn to talk?
group.pray: Ask for patience to listen well, and pray for the friends whose questions you have not yet heard.

sessions.title: Your own story, told honestly
teaching: The man born blind in John 9 was hauled before the religious authorities and questioned about theology he couldn't answer. He didn't pretend to. He told them what had happened: “There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see” (John 9:25). Your story works like that. It isn't a proof of the faith, and you shouldn't offer it as one, but it is honest evidence of what the faith has done in one life, and no one is better placed to give it than you.

Tell it the way you'd tell a friend what happened to you. Many Christians learned a polished testimony with a dark before and a bright after, and listeners can hear the polish. If you came to faith slowly, say so; many people do. If you still struggle, say that too. A story that ends with everything fixed is harder to believe than one that names what is still hard. Keep Christ at the center rather than yourself, and keep it short enough that the other person has room to ask.

open.label: How to Tell Your Story
open.why: A short guide to telling your own story plainly, without performance, including what to do if your coming to faith was quiet.

also.label: John 9, passage by passage
also.why: The whole account of the man born blind, who answered his questioners with what had happened to him.

also.label: Acts 26, passage by passage
also.why: Paul tells his own story before a king, plainly and in order, and lets it lead to Christ rather than to himself.

sessions.question: If you had three minutes to tell a friend how you came to trust Christ, what would you say first?
sessions.do: Write your story in no more than three hundred words: what life was like, how you came to Christ, and what is different now, including what is still hard. Read it aloud once.

verse.text: There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!

group.open: What did you think Christians were like before you became one, or before you took faith seriously?
discuss: Why might a quiet, ordinary story be more believable than a dramatic one?
What is still hard for you as a Christian, and would you be willing to say so when you tell your story?
How can you tell your story so that it points to Christ rather than to yourself?
group.pray: Give thanks for the people and moments God used to bring you to himself, and ask for honesty whenever you tell it.

sessions.title: The gospel in a few sentences
teaching: Paul summed up what he had received and passed on as of first importance: “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). It's worth being able to say the gospel just as briefly. One plain way has four movements. God made the world good and made us to know him. We turned from him, and the damage runs through every life and every society. Christ, God the Son, came, died in our place and rose again. And God calls us to turn and trust him, receiving as a gift what we could never earn.

Those four sentences summarize a longer story, and many people today need the story before the summary makes sense. The Bible runs from creation, through the fall, through Israel and the promises, to Christ, the church, and a new creation where God puts every broken thing right. Told that way, the gospel isn't a transaction plucked out of the air. It's the turning point of the one story the whole Bible tells. Learn to tell both: the short version for a moment at a bus stop, and the long one for a friend who has an evening.

open.label: The gospel in a minute
open.why: The good news in one short film, in plain words a child could follow, which is a fair test of whether you can say it simply too.

also.label: The whole Bible in two minutes
also.why: The whole story from creation to new creation in two minutes, the long version of the gospel told as briefly as it can be.

also.label: The Bible's story: Christ
also.why: The Study Bible's account of the story's turning point, with the passages that carry it, for when you want the long version in detail.

also.label: Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration: The Bible's Story
also.why: A longer guide to the four movements of the Bible's story, and how an ordinary life looks when it is lived inside that story.

sessions.question: Can you say the gospel in four sentences in your own words, and which of the four is hardest for you to put plainly?
sessions.do: Write the gospel in four sentences: God, us, Christ, and the response he asks. Then tell the whole Bible's story aloud in two minutes, to yourself or to a friend.

verse.text: For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: How would you have described the gospel before you understood it, if anyone had asked you?
discuss: Which of the four movements do people most often leave out when they explain the gospel, and what is lost?
Why might someone today need the whole story before the short summary makes sense?
When you take turns saying the gospel in four sentences, what do you notice in one another's words?
group.pray: Thank God for the good news in your own words, and ask for clarity to say it simply when someone asks.

sessions.title: Explaining the cross
teaching: The cross is the hardest part of the faith to explain and the part people most need explained. To many listeners it sounds like a father punishing his son, or like blood demanded by an angry god. Hear that objection out, because some Christians have described the cross in just those terms, and the objection is right to reject them. The New Testament says something stranger: that God himself, in the person of the Son, took on the cost of our wrong. “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

No single picture holds all of it, and the New Testament uses several. The cross is a sacrifice, echoing the lamb and the temple. It is a ransom that sets captives free. It is a substitution, the righteous for the unrighteous. It is a victory over the powers that hold the world. Churches have stressed different pictures in different ages, but all confess that the Son gave himself willingly, out of love, and that the Father, Son and Spirit were one in it. When you explain the cross, start with that love, and let the pictures fill it out.

open.label: The atonement, in the Study Bible
open.why: The Study Bible's doctrine study on what the cross accomplished, traced from the sacrifices of Israel to the letters, with the pictures Scripture uses.

also.label: Why did Jesus die?
also.why: A short film on why Jesus died, using the Bible's own pictures, made simple enough to watch with a child or a newcomer.

also.label: How salvation works
also.why: A short film on what God does to save and what he asks of us, useful for checking your own explanation against.

sessions.question: How would you answer a friend who says the cross sounds like a father punishing his son?
sessions.do: Write a paragraph explaining why Jesus died, for a friend who has never been to church. Use no word they would need a dictionary for.

verse.text: For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What did you first think when you heard that Jesus died for sins?
discuss: Which picture of the cross, sacrifice, ransom, substitution or victory, means most to you, and why?
Why does it matter to say that the Father, Son and Spirit were one at the cross rather than divided?
How would you explain the cross to someone who has never thought of themselves as needing forgiveness?
group.pray: Give thanks for the love shown at the cross, and ask for words that make it plain without making it small.

sessions.title: Explaining the resurrection
teaching: Everything else rests here, and Paul said so without hedging: “And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith” (1 Corinthians 15:14). When you explain the resurrection, you aren't describing a feeling the disciples had or a symbol of hope. You are making a claim about history: that the tomb was empty, and that Jesus was seen alive, in the body, by people who had watched him die. A skeptic is right to ask for reasons, and you should be glad when one does.

Give the strongest objection its due. The dead don't rise, and for many people that settles the matter before any evidence is heard. Others suggest that grief produced visions, or that the story grew in the telling. Then set out what needs explaining. Paul wrote down a list of witnesses within about twenty-five years of the crucifixion, and many historians who are not believers accept that Jesus' followers sincerely believed they had seen him. Say plainly that the evidence persuades many and not everyone. The question is which explanation best fits what happened.

open.label: Did the resurrection actually happen?
open.why: The site's Honest Answer on the resurrection, which states the skeptic's case fairly before weighing the evidence.

also.label: Was Jesus buried in a known tomb, and was it found empty?
also.why: A fuller piece from the case for the faith on the empty tomb and the explanations offered for it, for when a friend wants more.

also.label: Did Jesus Really Rise from the Dead?
also.why: A longer essay on the resurrection, for the reader who wants the whole argument and not only a summary of it.

sessions.question: What would you say to a friend who asks why you believe a dead man rose, without overstating the evidence or apologizing for it?
sessions.do: Write down the strongest objection to the resurrection you know, then three sentences answering it. Note honestly where your answer persuades you and where it doesn't yet.

verse.text: But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

care: Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When did the resurrection first seem like a real question to you rather than a story?
discuss: Why does Paul say the faith is worthless if Christ was not raised, and do you agree with him?
Which other explanation of the empty tomb seems strongest to you, and how would you answer it fairly?
How can you hold a firm belief in the resurrection and still respect a friend who isn't persuaded?
group.pray: Give thanks for the hope of the resurrection, and pray for anyone in the group who is grieving someone they love.

sessions.title: Explaining the Trinity simply
teaching: Christians worship one God, and they confess that the Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God: three persons, not three gods. Jesus sent his disciples to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), one name and three persons. The church didn't invent this to make the faith harder. It found it in the New Testament and spent the fourth century learning to say it carefully, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381, against teachers who made the Son a lesser being.

When you explain it, be careful with comparisons. Water, ice and steam, or one man who is a father, a son and a husband, both end up describing one God wearing three masks in turn, an old error the church rejected. It's better to say plainly that God is more than we can picture, and that the Trinity is less a puzzle than a description of love. If God is three persons who have loved one another forever, then love is older than the world. A friend may still find it strange. You are describing God, after all, not a machine.

open.label: How can God be three and one?
open.why: The site's Honest Answer on the Trinity, written for the person who finds the doctrine confusing or contradictory.

also.label: The Nicene Creed
also.why: The words the church settled on in the fourth century to say who the Father, Son and Spirit are, still confessed in churches across the world.

also.label: Who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit
also.why: A short film on the Trinity in plain words, a good model for explaining it to a child or a newcomer.

also.label: The Trinity, in the Study Bible
also.why: The doctrine study that traces the Trinity through the whole Bible, for when a friend asks where Scripture actually teaches it.

sessions.question: How would you explain the Trinity to a friend in a few sentences without using a comparison that breaks?
sessions.do: Read the Nicene Creed aloud slowly. Then write three sentences on the Trinity for a twelve-year-old, and check them against the creed.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

group.open: What comparison for the Trinity have you heard, and did it help or confuse you?
discuss: Why do common comparisons like water, ice and steam end up describing something other than the Trinity?
What difference does it make to say that love is older than the world?
Why might it be honest, rather than evasive, to admit that God is more than we can picture?
group.pray: Worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in your own words, and ask for wisdom to speak of God with reverence.

sessions.title: Explaining the Bible to someone who has never read it
teaching: To someone who has never opened it, the Bible looks like one long book of rules, and many who start at Genesis and read straight on give up somewhere in Leviticus. Explain first what it is: a library, sixty-six books in Protestant Bibles and more in Catholic and Orthodox ones, written over more than a thousand years in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, in poetry, law, history, letters and visions, that together tell one story. John said plainly why he wrote his Gospel: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

Then suggest a place to start. A Gospel is usually best, and Mark is short enough to read in an evening. Offer to read it with them, a chapter at a time and out loud, and let them ask the question they're embarrassed to ask. Don't defend every hard passage before they reach it, and don't pretend there are none. Philip met a man reading Isaiah on a desert road and began with a simple question: “Do you understand what you are reading?” (Acts 8:30). Then he sat beside him and started where the man already was.

open.label: What is the Bible?
open.why: A short guide to how the Bible is put together and how its many books make one whole, in words a newcomer can follow.

also.label: How to Open the Bible With People Who Have Never Read It
also.why: Practical help for the friend who has never read it: where to start, which translation to hand them, and why reading aloud together helps.

also.label: The Bible in a minute
also.why: The shape of the whole Bible in one minute, short enough to watch with a friend before you open it together.

sessions.question: If a friend asked you where to start reading the Bible, what would you say, and why?
sessions.do: Offer to read the Gospel of Mark with someone who has never read it, one chapter a week. If no one comes to mind yet, read Mark 1 aloud as if hearing it for the first time.

verse.text: But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.

group.open: What was your first experience of reading the Bible, and where did you start?
discuss: Why do so many first-time readers give up, and what would have helped them keep going?
Which hard passage are you most nervous a newcomer will ask about, and how might you answer honestly?
What did Philip do on the desert road that you could do with a friend?
group.pray: Ask God to open the Scriptures to the people you know, and for the patience to read alongside them.

sessions.title: Speaking with a friend of another faith or none
teaching: A Muslim neighbor, a Hindu coworker, a Jewish friend, an atheist brother: each comes with a whole way of seeing the world, and each deserves to be understood before being answered. Learn what they believe from them, not from a summary written by their critics, and name honestly what is true and good in what they hold. When Paul stood in Athens, he began with an altar he had seen in their city and quoted their own poets, and he still went on to speak plainly of Christ and the resurrection.

Respect has its own honesty. Don't pretend all religions say the same thing; most of their own believers would reject the claim, and it isn't true. Christianity makes a particular claim about Jesus that other faiths deny, and you can say so without contempt. So no tricks: no hidden agenda in a friendship, no argument built to corner someone, no push for a decision. Let your speech be gracious, as Paul told the Colossians, and leave your friend as free to disagree as you are to believe. A friendship that survives disagreement is a witness of its own.

open.label: Isn't it arrogant to say Jesus is the only way?
open.why: A piece from the case for the faith that states the objection at full strength, then weighs what Christians actually claim and why.

also.label: What do Christianity and Islam actually dispute?
also.why: An Honest Answer that sets out where the two faiths agree and where they truly differ, fairly to both.

also.label: How to Disagree Without Losing the Relationship
also.why: Help for holding your convictions and keeping your friends, when a conversation about faith turns into a real disagreement.

also.label: For skeptics
also.why: The room this site keeps for the skeptic, worth knowing well enough to send a friend there with confidence.

sessions.question: What does a friend of another faith, or of none, believe that you most need to understand before you speak?
sessions.do: Ask a friend of another faith or none what they believe and why, and what they find hardest about Christianity. Listen, thank them, and write down what you learned.

verse.text: Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

group.open: Who is a person of another faith or none whom you respect, and why?
discuss: Why does it matter to learn what someone believes from them rather than from their critics?
How can you say that Christianity's claims differ from other faiths without sounding contemptuous?
What would a friendship look like that survived a real disagreement about God?
group.pray: Pray by name for friends of other faiths or none, with gratitude for them, and ask for gracious speech.

sessions.title: Your own statement of what you believe
teaching: In the early church a person being baptized answered questions about the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and from those answers grew the words we call the Apostles' Creed. It was never meant to replace thinking. It gave believers a spine to think with, so that a farmer and a bishop could confess the same faith. You've spent this Academy reading the Bible's story, its doctrines and its hard questions. The closing work is to gather what you've learned into a statement of your own: what you believe, why you believe it, and what difference it makes, in words you would actually say aloud.

Write it in plain language, no longer than a page. Let the creed keep you inside the faith the church has always confessed, and let your own words carry the reasons and the life. Name where you still have questions. Then read it to one person who knows you, and ask whether it sounds like you. Paul, quoting a psalm, gave the reason anyone speaks at all: “I believed, therefore I have spoken” (2 Corinthians 4:13). What you write is not a finish line. It's the first draft of something you'll go on saying, and correcting, for the rest of your life.

open.label: The Apostles' Creed
open.why: The oldest common confession of the Western church, to keep beside you while you write so that your words stay inside the faith.

also.label: The family catechism
also.why: Short questions and answers on the faith, a model of how much can be said truly in a few plain sentences.

also.label: Next in Explain It: Teaching others the Bible
also.why: The next track in this program, for helping someone else grow: discipling one person, leading a group, and teaching children, teenagers and new believers.

sessions.question: In a page or less, what do you believe, why do you believe it, and what difference does it make?
sessions.do: Write your statement, no longer than one page, with the Apostles' Creed beside you. Read it aloud to one person who knows you well, and keep it where you will find it a year from now.

verse.text: And in keeping with what is written: “I believed, therefore I have spoken,” we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak,

group.open: What part of your statement was hardest to write, and why?
discuss: Why do you think the church has always needed short confessions like the creed?
As you read your statements aloud to one another, what do you hear in someone else's that you wish you had said?
What question did you name as still open, and how will you keep pursuing it?
group.pray: Give thanks for all you have learned through the Academy, and ask God to make your life and your words agree.
